body_markdown:
Have you ever bought a bag of frozen vegetables, only to find three more buried in the back of your freezer? Or maybe you’ve discovered a container of leftovers that you can’t even identify anymore. I have. Freezers are great for keeping food longer, but they’re also great at hiding things.


The easiest way to organize your freezer is to group similar foods together, use bins to keep everything in place, and label anything that isn’t in its original packaging. You don’t need an elaborate organizing system. A few changes can make it easier to find what you need, prevent duplicate grocery purchases, and[keep food from going to waste](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/keep-your-kitchen-organized-and-stop-wasting-food.html) .


## Key Takeaways


- Start by taking everything out of your freezer, getting rid of food you no longer want, and grouping similar items together.
- Organize frozen foods into categories, such as meat, vegetables, fruit, leftovers, and frozen meals.
- Use freezer-safe bins, baskets, or dividers to keep food from getting buried.
- Store food upright when possible so you can see more of what you have.
- Label containers and freezer bags with the contents and date.
- Keep older food toward the front so you’re more likely to use it first.
- Make a freezer inventory if you have a lot of food or a large chest freezer.


## Start by Cleaning Out Your Freezer


Before you start organizing, take everything out of your freezer and put it on the counter. If you have a lot of food, work in small sections or use an insulated cooler with ice packs to keep frozen food cold while you sort.


Then, group similar foods together so you can see exactly what you have. You may discover several bags of frozen broccoli, a stack of forgotten leftovers, or meat you bought months ago and never used.


As you sort, look for food that:


- Has damaged or torn packaging
- Has been in the freezer so long that its quality has noticeably declined (it’s a weird color, there’s ice all over it)
- Has severe freezer burn (Freezer burn doesn’t automatically make food unsafe, but it can affect the flavor and texture.)
- Has no label and can’t be identified
- You know you won’t use
- May have thawed and been stored at unsafe temperatures


Once you’ve sorted everything, wipe down any spills or crumbs before putting food back. Follow your freezer manufacturer’s cleaning instructions, and avoid using sharp tools to remove ice buildup.


## Group Similar Foods Together


The easiest way to stop food from disappearing is to give everything a designated spot. Instead of stacking frozen pizzas on top of vegetables and stuffing bags of fruit wherever they’ll fit, divide your freezer into categories.


Some useful categories include:


- **Meat and poultry:** Chicken, ground beef, steaks, pork, and other meats
- **Seafood:** Fish, shrimp, and other frozen seafood
- **Vegetables:** Broccoli, peas, corn, spinach, and mixed vegetables
- **Fruit:** Berries, mangoes, bananas, and smoothie ingredients
- **Frozen meals:** Pizzas, prepared dinners, and other ready-to-cook foods
- **Leftovers:** Soups, casseroles, sauces, and homemade meals
- **Bread and baked goods:** Bread, bagels, muffins, and rolls
- **Breakfast foods:** Waffles, pancakes, and breakfast sandwiches
- **Desserts:** Ice cream, frozen treats, and baked desserts
- **Miscellaneous:** Ice packs and other items that don’t fit into the main categories


You don’t need a separate bin for every category. If your freezer is small, combine groups that make sense for your household. For example, you might keep frozen fruit and vegetables in one section and all your frozen meals in another.


## Use Freezer Bins and Baskets


Bins and baskets can make a big difference when you’re trying to[keep frozen food organized](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/how-do-you-organize-your-fridge-and-freezer.html) . Instead of digging through loose bags and boxes, you can pull out a bin and see what’s inside.


Choose bins designed for freezer temperatures, though. Some regular plastic containers can become brittle and crack in the cold. And before buying organizers, measure your freezer’s shelves and drawers. Also, make sure the bins won’t block vents, prevent the door from closing, or make it difficult to remove food.


## Store Freezer Bags Upright


One of the best ways to organize freezer bags is to store them upright, almost like files in a filing cabinet. This works particularly well for soups, sauces, ground meat, chopped vegetables, and other foods that can be frozen flat.


Start by filling freezer-safe bags, removing excess air, and sealing them securely. Just make sure you don’t overfill the bags. Liquids expand as they freeze, so leave enough room to prevent leaks or splitting.


Then, lay the bags flat on a tray or baking sheet in the freezer until the contents are frozen solid. Then, stand them upright in a bin. A small corrugated cardboard box works, too. Instead of having a pile of bags stacked on top of each other, you’ll be able to flip through them to find what you need.


## Label Everything


If you’ve ever found a frozen container and wondered whether it contains chili, spaghetti sauce, or something else entirely, you know why labels matter.


Before freezing leftovers or repackaged food, write down:


- What the food is
- The date you froze it
- The number of servings, if helpful (0r if you even know)
- Any cooking or reheating instructions you want to remember


If you freeze similar foods regularly, such as several types of soup, be specific. A label that says “chicken tortilla soup” is much more useful than one that just says “soup.” For food in its original packaging, you may only need to write the purchase or freezing date somewhere easy to see.


Remember to use freezer-safe labels or a permanent marker that won’t rub off in cold temperatures. A little strip of masking tape and a Sharpie work for me.


## Use Square or Rectangular Containers


Square or rectangular freezer-safe containers are often easier to stack and arrange. They can also make better use of limited freezer space. Round containers work fine for freezing food, but they can leave awkward gaps when you’re trying to fit several of them on a shelf.


Don’t feel like you need to replace every container you own, though. Use what you already have and only buy new ones if your current storage system isn’t working.


## Keep Older Food in the Front


When you bring home groceries or freeze leftovers, try not to put the newest items in front of everything else. Move older food toward the front and place newer packages behind it. That way, you’re more likely to use what you already have before opening something new.


This is sometimes called the first-in, first-out method.


## Make an Eat-First Bin


If your freezer is packed, an eat-first bin can be especially helpful. Use a small basket or designate part of a shelf for food you want to use before anything else.


For example, you might put these items in your eat-first bin:


- Leftovers that have been frozen for several months
- Open bags of vegetables
- Half-used packages of frozen fruit
- Bread that’s been in the freezer for a while
- Homemade meals you want to use up
- Foods that are nearing their recommended freezer storage time for best quality


When you’re looking for something to make for dinner, check this bin first. You can also move food into the bin as you notice it getting older, rather than reorganizing the entire freezer.


## Organize a Top-Freezer Refrigerator


If your freezer is above your refrigerator, you probably have one or two shelves and a fairly small amount of storage space. The trick is to keep things from getting stacked so deeply that you can’t see what’s underneath.


Try these ideas:


- Use small bins to separate food categories.
- Keep frequently used foods near the front.
- Store flat packages upright when possible.
- Put larger boxes and bulky items toward the back.
- Use the freezer door for smaller items if your manufacturer’s instructions allow it.
- Avoid stacking food so high that it blocks air circulation.


If you have a wire shelf, you may want to use bins with solid bottoms to keep small packages from slipping through.


## Organize a Bottom-Freezer Drawer


Bottom-freezer drawers can hold a surprising amount of food, but they’re also good at hiding things underneath other things. If your freezer has multiple drawers or sliding baskets, assign a category to each section. For example, you might keep frozen vegetables and fruit in the upper drawer, with meat and prepared meals in the lower section.


Use smaller bins or dividers to separate foods within each drawer. This can keep bags from sliding into a pile every time you open and close the freezer. Try to keep frequently used foods in the upper or most accessible sections so you don’t have to dig through everything.


## Organize a Side-by-Side Freezer


Side-by-side refrigerator freezers usually have narrow shelves, which can make bulky packages difficult to store. Instead of piling everything wherever it fits, assign a purpose to each shelf.


For example:


- Top shelf: Frozen meals and leftovers
- Second shelf: Vegetables and fruit
- Third shelf: Meat and seafood
- Lower shelf: Bread and baked goods
- Bottom drawer: Extra or bulk foods


Adjust the categories based on what you actually buy. Small bins can help keep loose packages from falling over, while storing flatter packages upright may make narrow shelves easier to use.


## Organize a Chest Freezer


Chest freezers are great for storing large amounts of food, but finding something at the bottom can feel like an archaeological expedition. The easiest way to organize a chest freezer is to use baskets or bins that you can lift out.


Divide the freezer into sections and give each category a designated area. For example, you might keep beef on one side, poultry on another, and vegetables in a separate basket.


If you have multiple layers of storage, put foods you use most often in the top baskets. Keep less frequently used items in the lower sections.


You can also use different colored bins or large labels to make categories easier to identify.


Just make sure the containers don’t interfere with the freezer’s operation or prevent the lid from closing properly.


## Organize an Upright Freezer


An upright freezer can be easier to organize because everything is arranged on shelves, but food can still get pushed to the back and forgotten. Try assigning a category to each shelf. For example, one shelf might hold meat, another vegetables, and another prepared meals.


Use bins to keep smaller packages together and prevent items from falling out when you open the door. Keep heavier packages on sturdy lower shelves and avoid overloading the shelves or blocking air vents.


## Make a Freezer Inventory


If you have a large freezer or regularly buy groceries in bulk, keeping a freezer inventory can help prevent duplicate purchases. You don’t need a special app or spreadsheet. A sheet of paper taped to the freezer door can work just fine. Write down what you have and how much of it is in the freezer.


For example:


Food Quantity Date frozen


Ground beef 3 packages October 12


Chicken breasts 2 packages October 18


Frozen broccoli 4 bags October 20


Homemade chili 3 containers October 22


Strawberries 1 bag October 25


Update the list whenever you add or remove food. If you don’t want to keep track of every item, focus on foods you tend to buy in bulk or forget about, such as meat, vegetables, and leftovers.


## Freeze Food in Portions You’ll Actually Use


Large packages can take up a lot of freezer space, especially if you only need a small amount at a time. Before freezing food, think about how much your household usually eats in one meal. For example, if you typically cook one pound of ground beef at a time, divide a large package into one-pound portions before freezing it.


You can do the same with:


- Chicken breasts
- Ground meat
- Soup
- Chili
- Pasta sauce
- Cooked beans
- Bread
- Shredded cheese
- Chopped vegetables


Smaller portions are easier to organize, and you won’t have to thaw more food than you need.


## Remove Bulky Packaging When it Makes Sense


Some frozen foods come in large cardboard boxes that take up more space than the food inside. If the food is individually wrapped or sealed in freezer-safe packaging, you may be able to remove the outer box to save room.


Before throwing away the packaging, check whether it contains important cooking instructions, storage information, or a date you want to keep. You can always cut out the instructions and store them with the food or take a picture of them.


Don’t remove packaging that protects food from freezer burn or contamination. And if you repackage food, use containers or bags designed for freezer storage and label them clearly.


## Refrigerator Organization FAQs


### What is the best way to organize a freezer?


Group similar foods together, use freezer-safe bins or baskets to separate categories, and label everything that’s not in its original packaging. Keep frequently used foods easy to reach and older items toward the front so they don’t get forgotten.


### How do you organize a freezer without buying organizers?


Use the shelves and drawers you already have to create designated areas for different foods. Store freezer bags upright when possible, stack containers neatly, and label packages so you can find what you need. You can also reuse sturdy freezer-safe containers you already own.


### How do you organize a small freezer?


Focus on keeping food visible and easy to reach. Use a few small bins, store flat packages upright, and avoid bulky packaging when it isn’t needed. Keep foods you use most often in the easiest spots to access.


### How do you organize a deep freezer so food doesn’t get lost?


Use lift-out baskets or bins to divide food into categories. Store frequently used items near the top and less-used foods below. Keep an inventory so you know what’s at the bottom without having to dig through everything.


### What should go on the top shelf of a freezer?


The top shelf is often a convenient place for foods you use frequently, such as frozen vegetables, prepared meals, or leftovers. The best arrangement depends on your freezer’s design, airflow requirements, and how you use it.


### How long can food stay in the freezer?


Food kept continuously frozen at[0°F or below can remain safe indefinitely](https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/freezing-and-food-safety) , but its quality may decline over time. Different foods have different recommended storage times for best flavor and texture. Labeling food with the freezing date can help you use it while it’s still at its best.


### Can you use regular plastic bins in the freezer?


Some plastic bins may crack or become brittle at freezing temperatures. Look for bins labeled as freezer-safe or designed for low-temperature use. Make sure they fit without blocking air vents or preventing drawers and doors from closing.


### How often should you clean out your freezer?


Give your freezer a quick check every few weeks to look for forgotten food, open packages, and spills. A more thorough cleanout every few months can help you keep your inventory accurate and remove foods you no longer plan to use.
